Next, traverse the tree starting from the root using the characters of the search prefix. If a character is not found, return an empty list. From the node where the prefix ends, perform a depth first search to find all paths to nodes with the end flag. Maintain a list of pairs containing the current node and the accumulated string. Append the accumulated string to the results whenever an end flag is found. Return the results list. Example input: vocabulary of apple, apply, and banana, with prefix app. Expected output: list containing apple and apply.

title: Weighted Random Shuffler
spec: Write a function `shuffle(items, weights)` that takes a list of string identifiers and a list of corresponding positive float weights. The function must return a new list of the identifiers arranged in a random order, where the chance of picking an item next is proportional to its weight. Loop as many times as there are items. In each iteration, calculate the total sum of all weights currently remaining. Generate a random float between zero and this total sum. Iterate through the remaining items, keeping a running sum of their weights. When the running sum exceeds the random float, select that item. Remove the selected item and its weight from the remaining lists, and append the item to the final result list. Continue until all items have been selected. Return the result list. Example input: items a and b with weights ninety and ten. Expected output: a list of a and b, which will occur most of the time.

title: GeoHash Area Encoder
spec: Write a function `geohash(latitude, longitude, precision)` that takes a float latitude, a float longitude, and an integer character length. The function must compute the geohash string for the coordinates. Set the latitude range from negative ninety to positive ninety, and the longitude range from negative one hundred eighty to positive one hundred eighty. Maintain a boolean flag to alternate between longitude and latitude processing, starting with longitude. Loop to generate bits: find the midpoint of the current range. If the coordinate is greater than the midpoint, the bit is one and the lower bound becomes the midpoint. Otherwise, the bit is zero and the upper bound becomes the midpoint. Toggle the alternating flag. Group the generated bits into sets of five. Map each five bit integer to a character using the standard base thirty two string of digits and lowercase letters (excluding a, i, l, and o). Stop when the string reaches the requested length and return it. Example input: latitude zero, longitude zero, precision one. Expected output: the string s.

title: Histogram Equalizer
spec: Write a function `equalize(pixels)` that takes a list of integers from zero to two hundred fifty five representing grayscale image data. The function must apply histogram equalization and return a new list of adjusted pixel values. First, count the occurrences of each pixel value to create a frequency distribution list of size two hundred fifty six. Next, compute the cumulative sum of these frequencies. Find the minimum non zero cumulative sum. For each value from zero to two hundred fifty five, calculate a mapping to a new value: subtract the minimum from the cumulative sum, multiply by two hundred fifty five, divide by the total number of pixels minus the minimum, and round to the nearest integer. Finally, create the output list by replacing every original pixel with its mapped value. Return the new list. Example input: a list of identical dark pixels. Expected output: a list where all pixels are mapped to zero.

title: Infix to Postfix Converter
spec: Write a function `convert(expression)` that takes a list of string tokens representing a mathematical formula (numbers, basic arithmetic operators, and parentheses). The function must convert the sequence to reverse polish notation and return a new list of strings. Create an output list and an operator stack. Define a precedence order where multiplication and division are higher than addition and subtraction. Loop over each token. If it is a number, append it to the output. If it is an open parenthesis, push it to the stack. If it is a close parenthesis, pop operators from the stack into the output until an open parenthesis is popped and discarded. If it is an operator, pop operators from the stack into the output as long as their precedence is greater than or equal to the current operator, then push the current operator. After checking all tokens, pop any remaining operators to the output. Return the output list. Example input: tokens three, plus, four. Expected output: three, four, plus.

title: Jaccard Similarity Matrix
spec: Write a function `jaccard(sets)` that takes a list of lists of strings, where each inner list represents a collection of items. The function must calculate the Jaccard similarity between every possible pair of these collections and return a two dimensional list of floats. For every pair of lists, count how many unique strings appear in both lists to find the intersection size. Count the total number of unique strings across both lists to find the union size. Divide the intersection size by the union size to get the similarity score. If the union is empty, the score is one. Fill a grid where the row index and column index correspond to the indices of the collections, placing the computed score in each cell. Return this grid. Example input: a list containing two collections, one with apple and banana, and one with banana and cherry. Expected output: a two by two matrix with ones on the diagonal and zero point five elsewhere.

title: Mandelbrot ASCII Renderer
spec: Write a function `render(width, height, max)` that takes an integer image width, an integer image height, and an integer maximum iterations. The function must generate an ascii representation of the Mandelbrot set and return a list of strings, one for each row. Loop through the rows from zero to height minus one. For each row, construct a string by looping through the columns from zero to width minus one. Map the column index to a real number between negative two and one. Map the row index to an imaginary number between negative one and one. Starting with a complex number at zero, iteratively square it and add the mapped coordinate. Keep track of the number of steps. If the squared magnitude of the complex number exceeds four, stop iterating. Choose an ascii character based on the number of steps taken (a space for maximum steps, and increasingly dense characters for fewer steps). Append the row string to the final list. Example input: width ten, height ten, max ten. Expected output: list of ten strings forming a shape.

title: N Queens Solver
spec: Write a function `queens(size)` that takes an integer board dimension. The function must find all valid placements of queens on the board such that no two attack each other, and return them as a list of lists of integers. Each inner list represents a valid board, where the index is the row and the value is the column of the queen. Use a recursive backtracking search. Maintain a current board list. Iterate through possible columns for the current row. Check if placing a queen in the column conflicts with any previously placed queens by verifying if they share the same column or if the absolute difference in rows equals the absolute difference in columns. If safe, add the column to the board and proceed to the next row. If all rows are filled, add a copy of the board to the results list. Remove the last placement to explore other paths. Return the results. Example input: a size of four. Expected output: two valid board configurations.

title: Convex Polygon Intersector
spec: Write a function `intersect(subject, clip)` that takes two polygons, each defined as a list of coordinate arrays containing an x and y number. The function must return a new polygon representing their intersection using the standard clipping algorithm. Start with the subject polygon as the current output. Loop over every adjacent pair of vertices in the clip polygon to define an edge. For each edge, create an empty list for the next output. Loop over every adjacent pair of vertices in the current output polygon. Determine if the current point and the previous point are on the inner side of the clipping edge using the cross product. If both are inside, add the current point. If moving from outside to inside, compute the line intersection and add it, then add the current point. If moving from inside to outside, add only the intersection point. Update the current output and proceed to the next edge. Return the final output list. Example input: two overlapping squares. Expected output: a list of coordinate arrays forming the overlapping rectangular region.

title: ASCII Maze Generator
spec: Write a function `maze(width, height)` that takes two odd integers representing the grid dimensions. The function must generate a random perfect maze using depth first search and return it as a list of strings. Initialize a two dimensional grid of characters filled with hashes representing walls. Choose a starting coordinate at row one and column one, mark it as a space character to represent a path, and push it onto a coordinate stack. While the stack is not empty, look at the top coordinate. Identify all unvisited neighbors that are two cells away in the four cardinal directions. If there are valid neighbors, pick one randomly, mark the cell between the current coordinate and the neighbor as a space, mark the neighbor as a space, and push the neighbor onto the stack. If there are no unvisited neighbors, pop the current coordinate from the stack. Once finished, join the rows into strings and return the list. Example input: width five, height five. Expected output: a list of five strings forming walls and a continuous path.

title: Bank Interest Compounder
spec: Write a function `compound(principal, rate, years, additions)` that calculates the final balance of an investment. For each year, calculate the interest earned on the current balance and add it to the balance. After applying interest, add the constant yearly addition. Also track the total interest earned overall. Return an array containing the final balance and the total interest earned. For example, given a thousand dollars, a five percent rate, three years, and one hundred dollars added yearly, return the final amount and the total interest portion.

title: Recipe Nutrition Calculator
spec: Write a function `calculate(ingredients, database)` where ingredients is an array of pairs representing quantity and ingredient name, and database is an array of triplets representing ingredient name, calories per unit, and protein per unit. The function should calculate the total calories and total protein for the recipe. Also determine the ingredient that contributes the most calories and the ingredient that contributes the most protein. Return an array containing total calories, total protein, highest calorie ingredient name, and highest protein ingredient name. Example: if apple is fifty calories and one protein, and two apples are used, it adds one hundred calories and two protein.

title: Archery Tournament Scorer
spec: Write a function `score(arrows)` that takes an array of distances from the center for each arrow. The target has five zones: zero to two gets ten points, two to four gets eight points, four to six gets six points, six to eight gets four points, and eight to ten gets two points. Beyond ten gets zero points. Calculate the total score, the number of bullseyes scoring ten points, and the longest streak of consecutive bullseyes. Return an array with total score, bullseye count, and maximum bullseye streak. For example, distances of one, three, one, one, and twelve would give ten, eight, ten, ten, and zero points.

title: Employee Shift Scheduler
spec: Write a function `schedule(requests, available)` where requests is an array of pairs representing an employee name and their requested hours, and available is the total shift hours available to distribute. Allocate hours fairly by giving everyone one hour at a time in a round robin fashion until either the available hours are exhausted or all requests are fully met. Return an array of pairs containing the employee name and their allocated hours, followed by the remaining unallocated hours. For example, if three employees want five hours each and ten are available, they get four, three, and three hours respectively.

title: Frequent Flyer Tier Evaluator
spec: Write a function `evaluate(flights)` that takes an array of triplets representing flight distance, class multiplier, and airline partner status. Calculate the total qualifying miles by multiplying distance by the class multiplier. If the airline partner status is true, add a flat bonus of five hundred miles per flight. Determine the frequent flyer tier: over fifty thousand miles is gold, over twenty five thousand is silver, and otherwise bronze. Return an array containing the total qualifying miles, the tier name as a string, and the number of flights that earned more than two thousand miles.

title: Retail Inventory Value Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(shipments)` where shipments is an array of arrays representing individual deliveries. Each delivery contains the item name, quantity received, unit cost, and a perishability factor. Calculate the current value of each item by multiplying quantity by unit cost, then discounting by ten percent if the perishability factor is greater than five. Accumulate the total inventory value across all shipments. Also find the most valuable single delivery and the total number of highly perishable items. Return an array with the total value, the item name of the most valuable delivery, and the perishable count.

title: Marathon Split Time Analyzer
spec: Write a function `analyze(splits)` that processes an array of times in minutes for consecutive five kilometer segments of a marathon. Calculate the total finish time and the average time per segment. Identify the fastest segment time and the slowest segment time. Also compute the positive split, which is the difference in time between the second half of the race and the first half, assuming an even number of segments. Return an array containing the total time, average time, fastest segment, slowest segment, and the positive split difference.

title: Solar System Gravity Simulator
spec: Write a function `simulate(planets, time)` where planets is an array of triplets representing mass, current position, and current velocity in one dimension. For each unit of time up to the given limit, update the velocity of each planet by calculating the gravitational pull from all other planets, which is proportional to the other mass divided by the squared distance between them, with a sign indicating direction. Then update the position of each planet based on its new velocity. Prevent division by zero if positions are identical. Return an array of the final positions of all planets.

title: Cryptographic Hash Slicer
spec: Write a function `slice(message, size)` that takes a string message and an integer block size. Pad the message with trailing exclamation marks until its length is a multiple of the block size. Split the padded message into blocks. For each block, calculate a simple checksum by summing the character codes of its characters. Create a new array where each element is the checksum modulo two hundred fifty six. Finally, compute the average of these modular checksums. Return an array containing the padded string, the array of block checksums, and the average value.

title: Real Estate Mortgage Amortizer
spec: Write a function `amortize(principal, rate, payment)` that calculates the monthly breakdown of a fixed rate loan. The rate is given as an annual percentage. For each month, calculate the monthly interest by dividing the annual rate by twelve and multiplying by the remaining principal. The principal reduction is the fixed payment minus this monthly interest. Update the remaining principal. Continue until the principal reaches zero, adjusting the final payment if it overshoots. Return an array containing the total number of months, the total interest paid, and the amount of the final payment.

title: Podcast Episode Playlist Builder
spec: Write a function `build(episodes, limit)` where episodes is an array of pairs representing episode title and duration in minutes, and limit is a maximum total time. Iterate through the episodes and add them to a playlist array as long as the total duration does not exceed the limit. Count how many episodes were skipped because they would exceed the limit. Calculate the remaining time left under the limit after adding the episodes. Return an array containing the playlist of titles, the total duration used, the number of skipped episodes, and the remaining time.

title: Spacecraft Cargo Balancer
spec: Write a function `balance(containers, capacity)` where containers is an array of pairs representing cargo name and weight. The spacecraft has three separate holds, each with the given capacity limit. Distribute the containers one by one into the first hold that can accommodate the weight. If a container cannot fit in any hold, add its name to a leftover list. Track the total weight loaded into each hold. Return an array containing an array of three total weights for the holds, and the list of leftover container names.

title: Stock Dividend Reinvestor
spec: Write a function `reinvest(shares, price, dividends)` where dividends is an array of quarterly payout rates per share. For each quarter, calculate the total dividend payout by multiplying the number of shares by the payout rate. Buy as many whole new shares as possible with the payout using the given share price. Add these new shares to the total share count and carry over any remaining fractional cash to the next quarter. Return an array containing the final number of shares, the total dividend cash generated, and the remaining unused cash at the end.

title: Movie Theater Seating Optimizer
spec: Write a function `optimize(groups, rows, seats)` where groups is an array of group sizes, and rows and seats represent the dimensions of the theater. Keep track of the available consecutive seats in each row. For each group, search for the first row that has enough consecutive available seats. If found, deduct the group size from that row's available seats and increment a seated groups counter. If no row can fit the entire group together, increment a turned away groups counter. Return an array containing the seated groups count, the turned away groups count, and an array of remaining seats per row.

title: Board Game Dice Roller
spec: Write a function `roll(throws, sides)` where throws is the number of times to roll and sides is the number of faces on each die. Since we cannot use random numbers for tests, use a simple linear congruential generator starting with a seed of forty two, multiplying by sixteen thousand eight hundred seven, and taking the modulo of two billion one hundred forty seven million four hundred eighty three thousand six hundred forty seven. For each throw, use the generator to pick a value between one and the number of sides. Count the frequency of each face value. Return an array containing the frequency of each face and the longest consecutive run of the same face value.

title: Train Route Fare Estimator
spec: Write a function `compute(stations)` where stations is an array of pairs representing station name and its distance from the start of the line. The fare is calculated as a base fee of two dollars plus twenty five cents for every mile traveled between the first and last station in the array. However, if the total distance is over fifty miles, the rate drops to fifteen cents per mile for the portion exceeding fifty miles. Also apply a ten percent discount if the journey crosses more than five stations. Return an array containing the total distance traveled, the number of stations visited, and the final estimated fare.

title: Customer Loyalty Points Expirer
spec: Write a function `expire(transactions, current)` where transactions is an array of triplets representing points earned, points spent, and the month the transaction occurred. Current is the current month integer. Points expire twelve months after they are earned. To determine available points, process transactions chronologically. Spending points deducts from the oldest available unexpired earned points. At the current month, sum up all remaining earned points that are less than twelve months old. Return an array containing the total active points, the total expired points, and the total spent points.

title: Coffee Shop Queue Simulator
spec: Write a function `process(customers, baristas)` where customers is an array of preparation times for their orders, and baristas is the number of available workers. Maintain an array representing the time each barista will become free. For each customer, find the barista who will be free earliest. Assign the order to them, updating their free time by adding the customer's preparation time. Track the maximum wait time experienced by any customer before their order starts, and the total time until all orders are finished. Return an array containing the maximum wait time and the final completion time.

title: Smart Home Temperature Manager
spec: Write a function `manage(readings, target)` where readings is an array of hourly room temperatures. The system aims to keep the room near the target. For each reading, if the temperature is more than two degrees below target, the heater turns on, consuming three units of energy. If more than two degrees above, the air conditioner turns on, consuming four units. Otherwise, the system is idle and consumes one unit. Keep track of total energy consumed, the number of hours the heater was on, and the number of hours the AC was on. Return an array of these three values.

title: Spelling Bee Letter Scorer
spec: Write a function `judge(words, center)` where words is an array of guessed words and center is the required central letter. A word is valid if it contains the center letter and is at least four letters long. The score is one point for four letter words, and equal to the word length for longer words. If a word contains seven unique letters, it is a pangram and scores a bonus of seven points. Count the total score of valid words, the number of pangrams, and collect the valid words into a new list. Return an array with total score, pangram count, and the list of valid words.

title: Internet Bandwidth Throttler
spec: Write a function `throttle(requests, limit)` where requests is an array of data packet sizes in megabytes. The system processes requests sequentially. It maintains a token bucket that adds ten megabytes of allowance per step, up to a maximum equal to the given limit. For each request, if the packet size is less than or equal to the current allowance, it is transmitted and the allowance is reduced. Otherwise, the packet is dropped. Return an array containing the number of transmitted packets, the number of dropped packets, and the total megabytes successfully transmitted.

title: City Skyline Area Calculator
spec: Write a function `measure(buildings)` where buildings is an array of triplets representing the left coordinate, right coordinate, and height of each building. To find the total visible area, first determine the maximum right coordinate to define the width of the city. Create an array representing the maximum height at each integer coordinate. Iterate through each building, updating the city heights array with the maximum height for each segment the building covers. Finally, sum up all the heights in the array. Return an array containing the total visible area and the tallest recorded height.

title: Fleet Fuel Efficiency Tracker
spec: Write a function `track(vehicles)` where vehicles is an array of arrays. Each inner array contains the vehicle identifier, miles driven, and gallons of fuel used. Calculate the miles per gallon for each vehicle. Keep track of the total miles driven and total fuel used across the entire fleet to calculate the overall fleet efficiency. Find the identifier of the most efficient vehicle and the least efficient vehicle. Return an array containing the overall fleet miles per gallon, the best vehicle identifier, and the worst vehicle identifier.

title: Farm Crop Yield Predictor
spec: Write a function `predict(fields, rainfall)` where fields is an array of pairs representing crop type and acres planted, and rainfall is the seasonal rain in inches. Corn yields one hundred fifty bushels per acre base, soybeans yield fifty, and wheat yields eighty. If rainfall is below ten inches, corn yield drops by twenty percent and soybeans drop by ten percent. If rainfall exceeds twenty inches, wheat yield drops by fifteen percent. Calculate the total expected bushels for each of the three crop types across all fields. Return an array containing the total bushels of corn, soybeans, and wheat.

title: Video Game Level Grader
spec: Write a function `grade(attempts, par)` where attempts is an array of pairs representing the time taken and the number of enemies defeated by a player, and par is the target time for the level. Calculate a score for each attempt: start with one thousand points, subtract ten points for every second taken, and add fifty points for every enemy defeated. If the time is less than the par time, add a speed bonus of five hundred points. Keep track of the highest score, the lowest score, and the average score. Return an array containing the high score, low score, and average score.

title: Ice Hockey Standings
spec: A tournament tracks matches where a win gives three points, a tie gives one point to each team, and a loss gives zero points. If a match goes into overtime, the winner gets two points and the loser gets one point. The input to the entry function `rank(matches)` is a list of match records, where each record is a list containing the first team name, the first team goals, the second team name, the second team goals, and a boolean flag indicating if it went to overtime. The entry function must aggregate the total points for every team across all their matches. It must then return a list of team names sorted by their total points in descending order, using alphabetical order as a tiebreaker. For example, if the red team beats the blue team in regulation time, and the blue team beats the green team in overtime, the returned list will contain red, blue, and green in that order.

title: Bicycle Gear Calculator
spec: A bicycle has a set of front chainrings and rear cogs, each represented by their number of teeth. The gear ratio is the number of front teeth divided by the number of rear teeth. The entry function `gears(fronts, rears)` receives a list of front chainring tooth counts and a list of rear cog tooth counts. It must generate all possible combinations of gear ratios. Then, it filters out duplicate ratios, rounding each ratio to two decimal places. Finally, it sorts the unique ratios from lowest to highest and returns this sorted list of numbers. For example, given front teeth lists of forty and fifty, and rear lists of ten and twenty, the output is a list containing two, two and a half, four, and five.

title: Rollercoaster Ride Dispatcher
spec: A rollercoaster operates trains that can hold a maximum number of passengers. The ride manager receives a list of passenger groups, where each group is represented by the number of people in it. Groups cannot be split across different trains. The entry function `dispatch(groups, capacity)` must process the groups in their original order. If a group fits in the current train alongside previously boarded groups, they board it. If they do not fit, the current train is dispatched and a new train starts with that group. The function returns a list where each element represents a dispatched train and contains the total number of people on that train. For example, with groups of four, three, two, and five, and a train capacity of six, the output is a list containing four, five, and five.

title: Audio Sample Peak Normalizer
spec: An audio track consists of a list of numeric amplitude samples. Peak normalization scales these samples so that the maximum absolute amplitude reaches a specific target level without exceeding it. The entry function `normalize(samples, target)` takes a list of sample numbers and a positive target maximum value. It must first find the largest absolute value among all samples, returning a list of zeroes if that largest value is zero. Otherwise, it calculates a scaling factor by dividing the target maximum by that largest absolute value. It then multiplies every sample by the scaling factor, truncating each result to an integer towards zero, and returns the new list of samples. For example, given samples minus ten, five, and twenty, with a target of fifty, the output is minus twenty five, twelve, and fifty.

title: Quilt Fabric Piece Estimator
spec: A quilt is made of repeating square blocks, where each block requires a specific length of fabric cut from a standard roll. The entry function `estimate(blocks, width)` receives a list of required square dimensions for different block designs and the fixed width of the fabric roll. Each block must be cut as a single contiguous piece. The layout strategy places squares side by side along the roll width until the next square does not fit, at which point it starts a new row. The height of each row is determined by the largest square in that row. The function returns the total length of fabric required, which is the sum of the heights of all rows. For example, with block sizes of ten, twenty, fifteen, and five, and a roll width of thirty, the first row holds ten and twenty with a height of twenty, and the second row holds fifteen and five with a height of fifteen, resulting in a total length of thirty five.

title: Park Grill Placement
spec: A public park wants to install a shared barbecue grill that serves multiple picnic tables. The tables are located along a straight path, represented by a list of their distances from the park entrance. The entry function `locate(tables, range)` receives this list of distances and a maximum walking range. It needs to find a grill location that covers the maximum number of tables, meaning the distance between the grill and the table is less than or equal to the maximum walking range. To do this, the logic should consider every table location as a potential leftmost table covered by the grill, checking how many subsequent tables fall within twice the walking range from that start point. The function returns the maximum number of tables that can be served by a single grill. For example, with tables at one, five, nine, and twelve, and a walking range of three, placing a grill to cover a span of six units can cover tables at five and nine, resulting in a maximum of two covered tables.

title: Pottery Kiln Scheduler
spec: Fired pottery must be cooled gradually to prevent cracking. The entry function `cooldown(temperature, steps)` takes an initial firing temperature and a list of cooling steps, where each step is a list containing a cooling rate in degrees per hour and a target temperature for that step. The kiln cools down at the given rate until it reaches the target temperature, then moves to the next step. If a target temperature is higher than or equal to the current temperature, that step is ignored and skipped. The function calculates the time taken for each valid step by dividing the temperature difference by the cooling rate. It returns the total hours required to reach the final temperature, rounded down to the nearest integer. For example, starting at one thousand degrees, with steps of fifty degrees per hour down to five hundred, then twenty per hour down to one hundred, the total time is thirty hours.

title: Paint Hue Blender
spec: A painter mixes several colors, each represented by a list of three numbers denoting red, green, and blue intensities between zero and two hundred fifty five. The entry function `blend(paints)` takes a list of these color mixtures. To find the resulting blended color, the function must calculate the average of the red components, the average of the green components, and the average of the blue components separately. Before averaging, the total sum of each component must be accumulated across all colors in the list. Finally, each average must be rounded to the nearest whole number. The function returns a list of three numbers representing the final red, green, and blue values. For example, mixing pure red, which is two hundred fifty five, zero, zero, with pure blue, which is zero, zero, two hundred fifty five, results in one hundred twenty eight, zero, one hundred twenty eight.

title: Lawn Sprinkler Overlap
spec: A garden has multiple circular sprinklers. Each sprinkler is defined by a list of three numbers representing its horizontal coordinate, vertical coordinate, and watering radius. The entry function `overlap(sprinklers)` receives a list of these sprinklers. It must determine how many unique pairs of sprinklers have overlapping watering areas. Two sprinklers overlap if the distance between their centers is strictly less than the sum of their radii. The distance is found using the Pythagorean theorem on the coordinate differences. The function loops through all unique pairs of sprinklers, tallies the overlapping pairs, and returns this count as a single number. For example, if three sprinklers are at the origin with radius five, at ten units away with radius six, and at twenty units away with radius two, the first and second overlap, yielding a count of one.

title: Pinball Bumper Scorer
spec: The entry function `score(hits)` takes a list of strings representing the sequence of hit bumpers, either standard or multiplier. A standard bumper gives fifty base points. A multiplier bumper gives ten base points and also increases a running score multiplier by one for all subsequent hits. The multiplier starts at one. Furthermore, hitting three standard bumpers in an uninterrupted row awards an immediate bonus of five hundred points, after which the consecutive standard hit count resets to zero. A multiplier bumper interrupts the consecutive standard hits sequence. The function computes the total score by multiplying the base points of each hit by the current multiplier at the moment of impact, and adding any awarded bonuses. It returns the final total score as an integer. For example, hitting standard, multiplier, standard, and standard yields a total of two hundred and sixty points.

title: Wiper Speed Controller
spec: An automatic windshield wiper system adjusts its speed based on rain intensity. The entry function `wipers(rainfall)` takes a list of numbers representing rainfall measured in milliliters per minute over successive intervals. The system maintains a current wiper speed level starting at zero. For each interval, it calculates the average rainfall using the current measurement and up to two immediate previous measurements. If the calculated average is above ten, the speed increases by one, up to a maximum of three. If the average is below two, the speed decreases by one, down to a minimum of zero. Otherwise, the speed remains unchanged from the previous interval. The function collects the speed level during each interval and returns them as a list of integers. For example, if the moving averages for four consecutive intervals evaluate to five, twelve, twelve, and one, the speeds will be zero, one, two, and one.

title: Regatta Handicap Adjuster
spec: In a sailboat regatta, different classes of boats compete together using a handicap system. The entry function `adjust(boats)` takes a list of boat performances, where each item is a list containing the boat name, its elapsed time in minutes, and its assigned handicap rating. The corrected time is calculated by dividing the elapsed time by the handicap rating and then multiplying by one hundred. The function must compute the corrected time for each boat, round it down to the nearest integer, and then rank the boats. It returns a list of boat names ordered from the lowest corrected time to the highest. If two boats have the same corrected time, they are sorted alphabetically by name. For example, a boat taking sixty minutes with a rating of one hundred yields a corrected time of sixty, while a boat taking fifty minutes with a rating of eighty yields sixty two, making the first boat the winner.

title: Submarine Sonar Echoes
spec: A submarine uses sonar to map the ocean floor by sending sound pulses and timing the echoes. The entry function `echoes(pings)` receives a list of ping records, each containing an emission time in seconds, a return time in seconds, and an angle in degrees. The distance to the target is half the product of the time difference and the speed of sound, which is assumed to be one thousand five hundred meters per second. The function processes each record to calculate the distance. If the distance is less than fifty meters, it is flagged as a hazard. The function returns a list where each element is a list containing the calculated distance as an integer and a boolean indicating if it is a hazard. Invalid records where the return time is before the emission time must be ignored. For example, an emission at two seconds and return at four seconds gives a distance of one thousand five hundred meters and is not flagged as a hazard.

title: Meteor Shower Peak Finder
spec: Astronomers track the number of meteors seen per minute during a meteor shower. The entry function `meteors(observations, window)` takes a list of integer meteor counts for consecutive minutes and an integer window size. It must find the moving sum of meteor counts for every possible consecutive window of the given size. To find the peak activity period, it identifies the maximum sum found across all windows. The function returns a list containing the starting minute index of the peak window and the maximum sum. If there are multiple windows with the same maximum sum, it returns the index of the first one. For example, given counts of zero, two, five, three, one, and a window of three, the sums are seven, ten, and nine, so the peak starts at index one with a sum of ten.

title: Geode Crystallization Simulator
spec: A geode forms as layers of different minerals crystallize on its inner wall over time. The entry function `crystallize(minerals)` takes a list of mineral concentration values representing the surrounding fluid over successive days. Each day, if the concentration is above fifty, a crystal layer forms with a thickness equal to ten percent of the concentration, rounded down to an integer. If the concentration drops below twenty, the fluid becomes corrosive, dissolving one unit of the most recently formed layer. If the most recent layer is completely dissolved, it is removed from the geode entirely. The function simulates this process and returns a list representing the final sequence of crystal layer thicknesses from the oldest layer to the newest layer. For example, successive concentrations of sixty, eighty, ten, and ten will produce a final list of layers measuring six and six.

title: Coffee Roast Evaluator
spec: The flavor of roasted coffee depends on the temperature profile during roasting. The entry function `evaluate(temperatures)` receives a list of temperatures recorded every minute. The roasting process is divided into three phases. The drying phase occurs while the temperature is below one hundred fifty degrees. The browning phase is between one hundred fifty and two hundred degrees inclusive. The development phase is strictly above two hundred degrees. The function must calculate the number of minutes spent in each phase. A roast is considered balanced if the development phase duration is between fifteen and twenty five percent of the total roasting time inclusive. The function returns a list containing the three phase durations followed by a boolean indicating if the roast is balanced. For example, ten minutes drying, five minutes browning, and five minutes development yields a balanced roast because development is twenty five percent of the total time.

title: Greenhouse Mist Controller
spec: A greenhouse maintains humidity by spraying a fine mist when the air becomes too dry. The entry function `mist(readings, target)` takes a list of hourly humidity percentage readings and a target minimum humidity. The system operates a water tank with a capacity of one hundred liters, starting full. Every time the humidity drops below the target, the system sprays mist, which consumes five liters of water and increases the effective humidity for that hour by ten percent. If the tank is empty, it cannot spray. The function must return a list containing two values: the total number of times the mist was sprayed, and the final amount of water left in the tank. For example, with readings of forty, thirty, fifty, and twenty, and a target of thirty five, it sprays twice and leaves ninety liters of water in the tank.

title: Telescope Focus Calibrator
spec: An automated telescope sweeps through a range of focus motor positions, taking pictures and scoring their sharpness. The entry function `calibrate(sharpness)` receives a list of these sharpness scores in order of motor position. The true focus point is the position with the highest sharpness, but the data is noisy. The logic first applies a simple smoothing operation by replacing each score with the average of itself, the previous score, and the next score, truncated to an integer. The first and last scores are not smoothed and remain unchanged. Then, it searches the smoothed scores to find the highest value. The function returns the index of the highest smoothed score. If there is a tie, the lowest index is returned. For example, scores of ten, twenty, fifty, thirty, and ten will yield smoothed values where the highest is at index two.

title: Perfume Formula Scaler
spec: A perfumer creates fragrances by mixing base, heart, and top notes in specific proportions. The entry function `scale(notes, volume)` takes a list of note definitions, where each is a list containing a scent name and its relative parts by weight, along with a target total volume in milliliters. To scale the formula, the logic must first sum all the relative parts to find the total parts. Then, it calculates the volume for each note by multiplying the target volume by the note's parts and dividing by the total parts, rounding down to the nearest whole number. Because of rounding, the sum of the scaled volumes might be slightly less than the target volume. The function returns a list where each element is a list of the scent name and its calculated integer volume. For example, rose at two parts and jasmine at three parts for a fifty milliliter volume yields twenty and thirty.

title: Pigeon Loft Feeder
spec: A pigeon fancier houses different breeds of birds, each requiring a specific amount of seed mix per day. The entry function `feed(birds)` receives a list of bird records, where each record contains a breed name, the number of individuals, and the daily grams of seed required per individual. The automated dispenser drops seeds in batches of fifty grams. The logic must determine the total daily seed requirement for the entire loft by multiplying the number of individuals by their specific requirement and summing these up. Then, it calculates the number of full batches the dispenser must drop to meet or exceed this total. Finally, it determines the excess seeds that will be left over after dispensing the batches. The function returns a list containing the total seeds required, the number of batches, and the leftover excess. For example, ten birds needing two grams each and five birds needing four grams each requires forty grams total, triggering one fifty gram batch with ten grams left over.

title: Scuba Decompression Stops
spec: Deep scuba dives require controlled ascents with decompression stops at specific depths to prevent illness. The entry function `plan(depths)` takes a list of maximum depths reached during successive dive segments. The overall maximum depth of the entire dive dictates the decompression schedule. If the maximum depth is less than eighteen meters, no stops are needed. If it is between eighteen and thirty meters inclusive, a single stop at five meters for three minutes is required. If the depth exceeds thirty meters, two stops are needed: one at ten meters for five minutes, and one at five meters for ten minutes. The function evaluates the overall maximum depth and returns a list of required stops, where each stop is a list of depth and duration. For example, maximum depths of twenty and twenty five meters during a dive will dictate a single decompression stop at five meters for three minutes.

title: Balloon Altitude Adjuster
spec: A hot air balloon pilot controls altitude by burning fuel to rise or opening a vent to descend. The entry function `navigate(commands, fuel)` takes a list of string commands, which can be either burn or vent, and an initial amount of fuel in liters. The balloon starts at an altitude of zero. Each burn command uses two liters of fuel and increases the altitude by twenty meters. Each vent command uses no fuel and decreases the altitude by fifteen meters. The altitude cannot drop below zero. If a burn command is issued but there is not enough fuel, the command is ignored and the altitude slowly decreases by five meters due to cooling. The function processes the commands sequentially and returns a list containing the final altitude and the remaining fuel. For example, with three liters of fuel, issuing a burn command followed by a vent command leaves the altitude at five meters with one liter of fuel.

title: Sundae Flavor Combinations
spec: An ice cream parlor offers sundaes made by selecting exactly three different flavors from a menu. The entry function `mix(flavors)` receives a list of available flavor strings. The parlor wants to generate a menu of all possible three-flavor combinations. The order of flavors in a combination does not matter, so vanilla, chocolate, and strawberry is the same as chocolate, vanilla, and strawberry. The logic must iterate through the available flavors to construct unique triplets. It then joins each triplet into a single string with the flavors separated by a hyphen. The function returns a list of these joined combination strings. If the input list has fewer than three flavors, the function returns an empty list. For example, given mint, cherry, fudge, and caramel, it generates unique triplets like mint-cherry-fudge.

title: Fireworks Sequence Builder
spec: A pyrotechnics show relies on a precise timeline of fireworks launches. The entry function `sequence(fireworks)` takes a list of firework shell data, where each element is a list containing the shell type, the delay in seconds after the previous launch, and the flight duration in seconds. The logic must calculate the absolute launch time for each shell, starting the first launch at zero seconds. It must also calculate the explosion time for each shell by adding its flight duration to its absolute launch time. The function returns a list of formatted records, where each record is a list containing the shell type, the calculated launch time, and the explosion time. For example, a star shell with delay two and flight three, followed by a ring shell with delay four and flight two, will launch at two and six seconds, exploding at five and eight seconds respectively.

title: Sandcastle Wall Stability
spec: Building a large sandcastle requires assessing the stability of its outer walls based on their base width and height. The entry function `assess(walls)` takes a list of wall dimensions, where each item is a list containing the base width and the height in centimeters. A wall is considered stable if its base width is at least two thirds of its height. The logic must calculate the stability ratio for each wall. It then counts how many walls are stable and how many are unstable. Additionally, it identifies the height of the tallest stable wall. If no walls are stable, the tallest stable height is zero. The function returns a list containing the count of stable walls, the count of unstable walls, and the maximum stable height. For example, a wall with width ten and height twelve is stable, while a width of five and height of fifteen is not.

title: Workshop Material Cost Estimator
spec: You are to write a function `cost(materials, prices)` that computes the total cost of a building project. The first parameter is a list of required materials, where each entry is a list containing a material name and its required quantity. The second parameter is a list of bulk prices, where each entry is a list containing a material name, bulk quantity, and bulk price. The cost for each required material is calculated proportionally based on its bulk price. Loop through the required materials, find the matching bulk item, compute its unit price, and add the required cost to a running total. Finally, calculate a safety margin by adding ten percent to the total base cost. Return a list containing the base total and the total with the margin. For example, if the required list is [['wood', 500]] and bulk prices are [['wood', 1000, 2]], the output should be [1, 1.1].

title: Spacecraft Launch Trajectory
spec: Implement a function `trajectory(parameters, intervals)` to calculate the altitude and velocity of a rocket at various time intervals. The first parameter is a list of initial mass, fuel burn rate, and engine thrust. The second parameter is a list of time intervals in seconds. Assuming a constant gravity of nine point eight, iterate through the intervals. For each interval, calculate the new mass by subtracting the product of burn rate and time from the initial mass. Compute the upward acceleration as the thrust divided by the current mass, minus gravity. The interval velocity increase is acceleration multiplied by the interval time, and altitude increase is the velocity increase multiplied by the time. Return a list of lists representing velocity and altitude at the end of each interval. For example, an input of [100, 5, 2000] and [1, 2] should return [[10.2, 10.2], [20.6, 30.8]].

title: Parking Garage Allocator
spec: Create a function `park(vehicles, floors)` that assigns vehicles to parking levels based on height constraints. The first input is a list of vehicles, each being a list of plate number, height in meters, and parking duration in hours. The second input is a list of floors, each a list of floor level, maximum clearance height, and hourly rate. Iterate over the vehicles and assign each to the lowest level floor that has a clearance height strictly greater than the vehicle height. Compute the expected fee for the vehicle by multiplying its parking duration by that floor hourly rate. Maintain a count of parked vehicles and a sum of total expected revenue. Vehicles that do not fit on any floor are ignored. Return a list containing the total parked count and the total revenue. Example input [['ABC', 2.0, 3]] and [[1, 1.8, 5], [2, 2.2, 4]] returns [1, 12].

title: Data Center Switcher
spec: Write a function `route(packets, nodes)` that determines the next destination for network packets. The first parameter is a list of packets, where each is a list of packet identifier, source, destination, and payload size. The second parameter is a list of network nodes, each a list containing the node name, a list of connected node names, and its current load percentage. For each packet, look up the node matching its source. Find the connected node that has the lowest current load percentage. If there is a tie, pick the first one encountered. Store a pairing of the packet identifier and the chosen connected node. Return a list of these pairings. For example, routing [['p1', 'routerA', 'serverB', 100]] with nodes [['routerA', ['switch1', 'switch2'], 50], ['switch1', [], 80], ['switch2', [], 40]] returns [['p1', 'switch2']].

title: Travel Itinerary Linker
spec: Develop a function `link(segments)` that arranges unsorted flight segments into a continuous travel itinerary. The input is a list of flight segments, each represented as a list of origin city, destination city, and flight number. First, identify the starting city by finding an origin that does not appear as a destination in any segment. Next, build the itinerary in order by repeatedly finding the segment whose origin matches the current city, recording the flight number, and updating the current city to the new destination. Continue this process until no further segments match. Return a list of the flight numbers in the correct travel order. For example, input [['Paris', 'Berlin', 'AF2'], ['London', 'Paris', 'BA1']] returns ['BA1', 'AF2'].

title: Server CPU Monitor
spec: Create a function `monitor(readings, threshold)` that identifies sudden spikes in server load. The first argument is a list of hourly load percentages, and the second is a numeric jump threshold. Loop through the readings starting from the fourth hour. Calculate the average of the immediately preceding three readings. If the current reading is strictly greater than this average plus the threshold, mark the current hour index as a load spike warning. Collect all such hour indexes into a list. Return the list of warning indexes. For instance, given readings [40, 42, 41, 90, 45] and a threshold of 20, the output should be [3].

title: Concert Ticket Scaler
spec: Implement a function `price(tiers, remaining)` that dynamically adjusts event ticket prices. The first input is a list of seating tiers, each a list of tier name, base price, and total capacity. The second input is a list of currently remaining seats for each tier in the same order. For each tier, calculate the percentage of remaining seats by dividing the remaining seats by the total capacity. If less than twenty percent of seats remain, increase the base price by fifty percent. If more than eighty percent remain, decrease the base price by twenty percent. Otherwise, the price remains unchanged. Round all adjusted prices to the nearest whole number. Return a list of lists pairing each tier name with its adjusted price. For example, tiers [['VIP', 200, 10]] and remaining [1] should return [['VIP', 300]].

title: Courier Dispatch Planner
spec: Write a function `dispatch(packages, capacity)` that selects packages for a single delivery run. The first parameter is a list of packages, where each is a list of destination zone, weight in kilograms, and a priority level where higher numbers mean higher priority. The second parameter is the maximum weight capacity of the delivery vehicle. First, sort the packages in descending order of priority, breaking ties by ascending weight. Iterate through the sorted packages, adding their weight to a running total. If adding a package would exceed the maximum capacity, skip it and check the next one. Collect the destination zones of all included packages. Return a list of these destination zones. Example input [['North', 5, 1], ['South', 3, 2]] and capacity 4 returns ['South'].

title: Film Casting Director
spec: Design a function `casting(roles, actors)` that allocates actors to movie roles. The first parameter is a list of roles, each a list of character archetype, required acting level, and screen time. The second parameter is a list of actors, each a list of actor name, specialization, and their maximum acting level. For every role, find the available actors whose specialization exactly matches the character archetype and whose maximum acting level is greater than or equal to the required acting level. From these eligible candidates, pick the one with the lowest maximum acting level to save the top actors for more demanding roles. Return a list of lists, pairing each archetype with the chosen actor name.

title: Reef Tank Doser
spec: Construct a function `dose(parameters)` that calculates the required volume of chemical additives for an aquarium. The input is a list of three current water parameters: calcium, alkalinity, and magnesium. The target levels are four hundred twenty for calcium, eight for alkalinity, and thirteen hundred for magnesium. Calculate the deficit for each parameter by subtracting the current level from the target, ensuring no deficit is negative. Multiply the calcium deficit by two to get milliliters of calcium additive. Multiply the alkalinity deficit by five for alkalinity additive, and the magnesium deficit by three for magnesium additive. Return a list of the three required additive volumes in milliliters. Example input [400, 7, 1250] returns [40, 5, 150].

title: Amusement Park Revenue Assessor
spec: Write a function `revenue(tickets, food)` to calculate total daily takings at a park. The first parameter is a list of ticket sales, each a list of visitor category and quantity sold. The categories are adult at fifty dollars, child at thirty dollars, and senior at forty dollars. The second parameter is a list of food shop registers, each a list of shop name and total cash taken. Loop through the tickets and multiply the quantity by the correct price to get total ticket revenue. Sum the cash taken from all food shops. Add the ticket revenue and food revenue to get the gross revenue. Calculate an eight percent tax deduction on the gross revenue to find the net revenue. Return a list containing the gross revenue and net revenue.

title: Ferry Deck Weight Balancer
spec: Develop a function `balance(vehicles)` that calculates the center of gravity for a loaded car ferry. The input is a list of vehicles, where each is a list containing its weight in tons, its position from the bow in meters, and its position from the port side in meters. Initialize accumulators for total weight, total bow moments, and total port moments. Iterate through the vehicles, adding the weight to the total weight. For each vehicle, multiply its weight by its bow position and add it to bow moments, then multiply its weight by its port position and add it to port moments. Finally, divide the total bow moments and total port moments by the total weight to find the average positions. Return a list of total weight, average bow position, and average port position.

title: Zoo Animal Diet Planner
spec: Create a function `diet(animals)` that computes the weekly food order for a zoo. The input is a list of animal groups, where each entry is a list of species name, number of animals in the group, daily meat requirement per animal in kilograms, and daily produce requirement per animal in kilograms. For each group, multiply the number of animals by their daily meat and produce requirements, then multiply by seven to get weekly amounts. Maintain a running sum of total meat and total produce required across all groups. Add a five percent spoilage buffer to both totals and round up to the nearest whole number. Return a list of total weekly meat and total weekly produce.

title: Hiking Trail Assessor
spec: Write a function `trail(segments)` that estimates the completion time for a mountain hike. The input is a list of route segments, each represented as a list of distance in kilometers and elevation gain in meters. Initialize totals for distance, elevation, and time. For each segment, add its distance and elevation to the respective totals. Calculate the segment base time in minutes by dividing its distance by a flat walking speed of five kilometers per hour, then multiplying by sixty. Add a penalty of fifteen minutes for every one hundred meters of elevation gain in that segment. Accumulate this estimated time. Return a list of total distance, total elevation, and total time in minutes. Example input [[5, 200]] returns [5, 200, 90].

title: Snowboard Rental Tracker
spec: Implement a function `rentals(customers, inventory)` to assign snowboards to riders. The first input is a list of customers, each a list of customer name and height in centimeters. The second input is a list of available snowboards, each a list of board identifier and length in centimeters. Sort the inventory so that board lengths are in ascending order. Loop through each customer and calculate their minimum board length, which is eighty percent of their height. Find the first available board that meets or exceeds this minimum length. Assign the board, mark it as unavailable for future customers, and store the pairing of customer name and board identifier. Return a list of these pairings in the same order as the customers.

title: Microgrid Battery Manager
spec: Create a function `microgrid(loads, solar, battery)` to simulate a household energy system. The first parameter is a list of hourly electricity loads, the second is a list of hourly solar generation, and the third is the initial battery charge level. The battery has a maximum capacity of one hundred units. Loop through the twenty four hours. Calculate the net load by subtracting the solar generation from the electricity load. If the net load is positive, subtract it from the battery charge, and if the battery drops below zero, add the shortfall to a running total of unmet load and reset the battery to zero. If the net load is negative, add the surplus to the battery, capping it at the maximum capacity. Return a list of final battery charge and total unmet load.

title: Art Auction Hammer
spec: Write a function `auction(lots)` that processes the results of an art sale. The input is a list of auction lots, where each lot is a list containing the lot identifier, the reserve price, and the highest bid received. A lot is considered sold if the highest bid is greater than or equal to the reserve price. For each sold lot, calculate the buyer premium as twenty percent of the highest bid, and the auctioneer commission as ten percent of the highest bid. Keep running totals of the hammer price, total buyer premiums, and total commissions across all sold lots. Unsold lots contribute nothing. Return a list of these three totals. Example input [['lot1', 100, 150], ['lot2', 200, 100]] returns [150, 30, 15].

title: Airline Baggage Assessor
spec: Develop a function `baggage(passengers, limit)` to calculate overage fees for airline luggage. The first parameter is a list of passengers, where each is a list containing a passenger name and a list of individual bag weights. The second parameter is the maximum weight allowed per bag. Iterate over each passenger and check their bag weights. For any bag that strictly exceeds the weight limit, calculate an overweight fee consisting of a fifty dollar flat charge plus two dollars for every kilogram over the limit. Accumulate the fees for all bags belonging to a passenger. Return a list of lists, pairing each passenger name with their total calculated fee.

title: Haunted House Spacer
spec: Design a function `spacing(groups, speed)` to determine entry times for haunted house visitors. The first parameter is a list of guest groups, each a list of group name and their walking speed in meters per minute. The second parameter is the standard base interval of two minutes. Initialize the current clock time at zero and store it for the first group. For each subsequent group, compare their speed to the immediately preceding group. If the previous group is strictly slower, add an extra minute to the standard base interval. Add this final interval to the current clock time and record it for the group. Return a list of dispatch times in minutes from the start. Example input [['A', 50], ['B', 40], ['C', 60]] and base 2 returns [0, 2, 5].

title: Resort Housekeeping Dispatcher
spec: Write a function `housekeeping(rooms, staff)` to estimate the daily workload for cleaning staff. The first input is a list of room records, each a list of room number and status, where status is either checkout or stayover. The second input is the number of available cleaning staff. Iterate over the rooms to calculate the total required cleaning minutes. A checkout room requires forty five minutes of cleaning time, whereas a stayover room requires fifteen minutes. Sum all these minutes together. Then, divide the total minutes by the number of available staff to find the expected workload per person. Return a list containing the total required minutes and the workload per staff member. Example [['101', 'checkout'], ['102', 'stayover']] and 2 returns [60, 30].

title: Canal Lock Tariff Calculator
spec: Create a function `tariff(transits, rates)` that computes the fees for boats using a canal system. The first argument is a list of boat transits, each a list of vessel registration, distance traveled in kilometers, and vessel class. The second argument is a list of tariff rates, each a list of vessel class and the cost per kilometer. For each transit, locate the corresponding rate for the vessel class. Multiply the transit distance by that unit rate to find the base fee. If the vessel class is commercial, apply a twenty percent surcharge to the base fee. Accumulate the final fee amounts for all transits into a grand total. Return the total fees collected. Example transits [['XYZ', 10, 'yacht']] and rates [['yacht', 2], ['commercial', 5]] returns 20.

title: Cosmetics Factory Batcher
spec: Implement a function `cosmetics(batches)` to calculate the bulk ingredients required for skin cream production. The input is a list of production batches, where each is a list of product name, desired output weight in kilograms, and a boolean indicating if it requires fragrance. For every kilogram of desired output, the recipe requires zero point six kilograms of base lotion and zero point four kilograms of purified water. If the batch requires fragrance, it also requires zero point zero five kilograms of essential oil per kilogram of output. Iterate through the batches to accumulate the total weight of base lotion, purified water, and essential oil needed. Return a list containing total base lotion, total water, and total essential oil.

title: Warehouse Order Picker
spec: Develop a function `picker(orders, layout)` that calculates the total distance and weight handled. The first parameter is a list of ordered items, each a list containing the item identifier and quantity. The second parameter is a list of warehouse bins, each a list containing the item identifier, its distance from the origin in meters, and the weight of a single unit in kilograms. The picker starts at distance zero with a total carried weight of zero and a total distance of zero. Iterate through the ordered items. For each item, find its bin in the layout. Calculate the distance moved from the current location to the bin, and add it to the total distance. Update the current location. Calculate the weight of the picked items by multiplying quantity by unit weight, and add it to the carried weight. Finally, add the distance to return to the origin. Return a list of total distance and total weight.

title: Highrise Window Washer
spec: Write a function `washer(windows, speed)` to estimate the time needed to clean the exterior of a building. The first parameter is a list of building faces, each a list of width in meters and height in meters. The second parameter is the cleaning speed in square meters per hour. Initialize a variable for total glass area and one for total setup time. Loop through the building faces, multiplying the width by the height to find the face area, and add it to the total area. For each face, add two hours to the setup time. Divide the total glass area by the cleaning speed to get the base washing time, then add the setup time. Return a list of total area and total estimated hours.

title: Vineyard Harvest Estimator
spec: Create a function `harvest(blocks)` that predicts the juice yield from a vineyard. The input is a list of vineyard blocks, each a list containing a block identifier, number of vines, average clusters per vine, and average berry weight in grams. Assume each cluster contains one hundred berries. Iterate over the blocks. For each block, find the total number of clusters by multiplying the vine count by the average clusters per vine. Find the total grape weight in grams by multiplying the total clusters, one hundred, and the berry weight. Convert the weight to kilograms by dividing by one thousand. Assume every kilogram of grapes yields zero point seven liters of juice. Return a list of lists pairing each block identifier with its estimated liters of juice.

title: Beekeeping Nectar Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(hives)`. The input is a list of hives where each hive has a population count, an active foragers percentage, a local temperature in celsius, and a location modifier. If the temperature is above thirty degrees, subtract zero point five from the location modifier. Calculate the daily nectar gathered by multiplying the population by the foragers percentage, then by the location modifier, and finally by a base collection rate of two and a half grams. Calculate a daily maintenance cost equal to five percent of the total population in grams of nectar. Subtract this cost from the gathered nectar. If the location modifier is below zero point eight, the hive consumes an additional ten percent of its remaining gathered nectar. Return a list containing the total net gathered nectar across all hives rounded to the nearest integer, and the index of the most productive hive. For example, given a hive with ten thousand bees, twenty percent foragers, thirty five degrees, and a modifier of one point five, it returns roughly four thousand and zero.

title: Bookbinding Cost Estimator
spec: Implement `bind(books)`. The input is a list of book orders, where each specifies a page count, a height in inches, a width in inches, a title string, and a cover material. Calculate the material cost for each book. Paper costs zero point zero five dollars per page. The cover area is twice the height times the width, plus a spine area calculated as page count divided by two hundred times the height. Cover materials cost two dollars per square inch for leather, one dollar for cloth, and zero point five for paper. Add a flat thread cost of one dollar per book, and a stamping cost of zero point ten dollars per character in the title. Calculate the total weight of the book in ounces, assuming each page is zero point one ounces and the cover is two ounces. The function must return a list of total costs for each book, rounded to two decimal places. For a one hundred page book measuring eight by five with a paper cover and a five letter title, the cost should be forty eight point six three.

title: Mushroom Foraging Scorer
spec: Create `score(mushrooms)`. The input is a list of mushrooms, each having a gross weight in grams, a toxicity level from zero to ten, and a bug damage percentage. Filter out any mushroom with a toxicity level above three or bug damage over thirty percent. For the remaining safe mushrooms, calculate the base weight by subtracting the bug damage percentage applied to the gross weight. Then subtract a soil penalty of five grams per mushroom. If the base weight becomes negative, set it to zero. Calculate an edibility score by multiplying the base weight by a flavor multiplier based on toxicity where zero is worth five points, one is three points, two is two points, and three is one point. The function must return a list with two values: the total final base weight and the sum of all edibility scores. For instance, a hundred gram mushroom with zero toxicity and ten percent damage yields eighty five grams and four hundred twenty five score points.

title: Tea Blending Optimizer
spec: Write `blend(target)`. The input is a list of three desired flavor intensities for astringency, sweetness, and earthiness, each on a scale from zero to one hundred. Three base teas are available: black tea has astringency eighty, sweetness ten, earthiness forty, and costs two dollars per ten grams; green tea has astringency forty, sweetness sixty, earthiness thirty, and costs three dollars; herbal tea has astringency ten, sweetness ninety, earthiness ten, and costs four dollars. Calculate the absolute difference between each base tea profile and the target profile by summing the differences across all three flavor dimensions. Find the base tea with the lowest total difference. The blend will use seventy percent of the closest matching tea, twenty percent of the second closest, and ten percent of the furthest. Calculate the total cost to produce one hundred grams of this specific blend. Return a list containing the three tea weights and the total cost in dollars. For a target of fifty, fifty, fifty, the total cost depends on the selected blend ratios.

title: Kite Flying Tension
spec: Develop `tension(conditions)`. The input is a list of atmospheric conditions including wind speed in meters per second, air density, and kite surface area in square meters. Compute the aerodynamic lift and drag. Lift is calculated as half the air density times wind speed squared times the surface area times a lift coefficient of one point two. Drag is calculated similarly but with a drag coefficient of zero point eight. Calculate the line sag force, which is the air density times the surface area divided by the wind speed, multiplied by ten. The total string tension is the square root of the sum of the squares of lift and drag, plus the line sag force. If the tension exceeds five hundred newtons, the string breaks. Return a list containing a boolean indicating if the string holds, and the calculated tension rounded to the nearest integer. For wind speed ten, density one point two, and area two, the output should be true and roughly one hundred seventy five.

title: Clock Escapement Simulator
spec: Write a function `tick(pendulums)`. The input is a list of pendulum configurations where each has a length in meters and a bob mass in kilograms. For each configuration, calculate the period of the pendulum using the formula two times pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity, assuming gravity is nine point eight one. The base energy required to maintain the swing is the mass times gravity times the length times the cosine of a drop angle of zero point one radians. Calculate the air resistance loss, which is the bob mass times the square of the length multiplied by zero point zero five. Deduct this loss from the base energy. Calculate how many ticks occur in one hour by dividing thirty six thousand by the period. Return a list containing the total number of ticks for the first configuration and its total adjusted energy required. For a length of one meter and mass of one kilogram, it returns approximately one thousand eight hundred ticks and nine point six energy.

title: Baguette Baking Schedule
spec: Implement `schedule(doughs)`. The input is a list of dough preparations containing ambient temperature in celsius, yeast percentage, and hydration percentage. Calculate the total time required from mixing to baking. The base proofing time is one hundred and twenty minutes. For every degree above twenty celsius, subtract five minutes, and for every degree below, add ten minutes. If the yeast percentage is below one, increase the current calculated time by thirty percent. If hydration is above seventy five percent, add a folding rest period of forty five minutes. Determine the final oven temperature, which starts at two hundred and fifty degrees, but decreases by ten degrees for every percentage point of yeast above one. Return a list of total processing times in minutes and the final oven temperatures for each dough preparation. For a temperature of twenty two, one point two yeast, and seventy hydration, the time is one hundred and ten minutes and the oven is two hundred and forty eight degrees.

title: Soap Curing Predictor
spec: Create `cure(batches)`. The input is a list of soap batches with starting weight in grams, water discount percentage, and average curing humidity. Calculate the final weight of each batch after four weeks. The initial water weight is thirty percent of the starting weight, reduced by the water discount percentage. During curing, the soap loses a fraction of its water weight equal to ninety minus the average humidity, divided by one hundred. Determine the lost water weight and subtract it from the starting weight. Calculate the lye required, which is fifteen percent of the starting weight, and subtract the water discount percentage from the lye amount as well. If the final weight falls below eighty percent of the starting weight, the batch is marked as overcured. The function returns a list where each element is the final weight rounded down to the nearest gram, alongside the lye required. For a thousand gram batch, zero discount, and fifty humidity, the final weight is eight hundred and eighty grams, and lye is one hundred and fifty.

title: Origami Crease Estimator
spec: Write `fold(designs)`. The input is a list of origami design plans, each having a base type string, a number of points, and a detail level integer. A bird base starts with sixteen creases, a frog base with twenty four, and any other base with eight. The total creases equal the starting creases plus the number of points squared times the detail level. The paper thickness at the densest point doubles for every ten creases, starting at a base thickness of zero point one millimeters. Calculate the estimated folding time in minutes, which is the total creases multiplied by zero point five, plus the maximum thickness multiplied by two. The function should calculate the total creases, the maximum thickness, and the folding time for each design. Return a list of maximum thicknesses and folding times rounded to two decimal places. For a bird base with four points and detail level two, the creases are forty eight, the thickness is one point six, and the time is twenty seven point two.

title: Tapestry Weaving Yarn Calculator
spec: Implement `weave(tapestries)`. The input is a list of projects specifying width in inches, length in inches, ends per inch, picks per inch, and a pattern complexity boolean. Calculate the yardage of warp and weft yarn needed. Warp yardage is the width times ends per inch times the length plus a ten inch fringe on both sides, divided by thirty six. Weft yardage is the width times picks per inch times the length, divided by thirty six. Because weaving shrinks the fabric, add ten percent to both yardages. Calculate the total number of heddles required, which is the width multiplied by the ends per inch. If the pattern is complex, double the heddle count. Return a list containing the total warp yardage, total weft yardage, and total heddles required across all projects, with yardages rounded up to the nearest whole yard. For a ten by twenty inch simple project with eight ends and twelve picks, the output is nine warp yards, forty weft yards, and eighty heddles.

title: Cheese Aging Inspector
spec: Create `inspect(wheels)`. The input is a list of cheese wheels, each with an initial weight in kilograms, an aging duration in months, and a target moisture loss percentage. Each month, a wheel loses one point five percent of its current weight. After the full aging duration, calculate the total percentage of weight lost based on the initial weight. If the actual weight loss meets or exceeds the target moisture loss percentage, and the aging duration is at least six months, the wheel is ready. Calculate the selling price for ready wheels, which is twenty dollars per kilogram of final weight, plus a premium of five dollars if the aging duration exceeds twelve months.
